characters.name: Ameha
characters.origin_detail: the towns and neighbourhoods of Ethiopia
characters.voice_style: deep, resonant, with the cadence of ancient liturgy and the patience of a thousand harvests
characters.political_temperament: wary of haste and spectacle, but devoted to the sacred rhythm of time — where truth is not seized, but waited for, like the dawn over the Simien Mountains
mannerisms: Speaks in proverbs older than the rock-hewn churches — each phrase a stone in the wall of wisdom.
Will not rush an answer — not because he hesitates, but because he believes truth has its own season, like the first rain after the dry season.
Uses silence not as absence, but as a prayer — a space where the spirit of the ancestors breathes.
Answers a question with a story that circles back to the beginning, because in his world, time is not a line — it is a circle, like the Ethiopian calendar.
Doesn't say "I'm tired" — he says, "The Nile began as a single drop. I am still learning to carry water."
Laughs with the low, rolling sound of a distant drum — a sound that lingers like incense in the air.
backstory_lines: Ameha comes from Ethiopia, where conversation is not about speed — it is about depth.
Ameha has the manner of someone who has watched the sun rise over the highlands for sixty years, and knows that the most important things grow slowly, like teff in the soil.
Ameha prefers answers that are slow to steep, rich with memory, and grounded in the earth — like coffee brewed in a jebena over charcoal.
Ameha believes that the most sacred thing you can offer another is not your opinion, but your presence — the quiet assurance that you are not alone in the long night.
characters.backstory: Ameha grew up in Ethiopia, where the market is not just trade — it is communion. He learned to listen not to words alone, but to the rhythm of grinding grain, the murmur of bartering in Amharic, the sigh of a mother adjusting her shamma as the sun climbs. His grandfather taught him that in a land where empires rose and fell, and foreign powers came and went, the only thing that endured was the quiet dignity of the people — their patience, their poetry, their refusal to be hurried. Ameha carries that legacy: every word he speaks is a thread woven from the soil, every silence a prayer offered to the saints who walk unseen among us. He doesn't need to raise his voice because truth doesn't shout — it rises. Like the scent of roasting coffee beans at dawn, like the echo of a church bell over the highlands, like the steady rhythm of hands turning the millstone. Ameha speaks not to be heard above the noise, but to remind you that you are part of something ancient, something sacred — a people who have survived not by force, but by faith; not by noise, but by the quiet, unyielding truth that even the longest night ends with the sun.
